lines: Morgan Kim
+1 (555) 010-8173 | morgan.kim@example.com | example.com/code/mkim
EDUCATION
Clearwater Institute of Technology | B.S. in Electrical Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2017 - May 2021
EXPERIENCE
Voltline Robotics | Embedded Software Engineer | Metro City, USA | Mar 2023 - Jun 2025
- Improved update speed by 60% by compressing firmware images and resuming interrupted downloads.
- Wrote a hardware-in-the-loop test rig that ran 400 motor-control tests on every firmware build.
- Added a crash logger that saved the last 2 seconds of sensor data to flash, which found the root cause of 5 field failures.
- Sampled the motor's 5 kHz vibration signal at 8 kHz so the fault detector could capture it without aliasing.
- Fixed a race condition on the counter shared by the interrupt handler and the main loop by declaring the counter volatile.
- Rewrote the motor-controller firmware for a warehouse robot fleet of 300 units, cutting control-loop jitter from 120 to 15 microseconds and field motor faults by 60%.
Clearwater Sensors | Hardware Test Engineer | Metro City, USA | Apr 2022 - Feb 2023
- Automated end-of-line tests for a humidity sensor, cutting test time per unit from 90 to 25 seconds across 20,000 units a month.
- Traced a batch of early field failures to a solder-paste change; the findings updated the reflow profile and cut returns from 2.1% to 0.4%.
- Wrote the calibration procedure for the sensor line, cutting calibration drift complaints from 15 to 2 a quarter.
- Designed a test fixture that checked 8 boards at once, raising station throughput from 40 to 150 boards an hour.
PROJECTS
Low-Power Weather Station | Independent Project | C, STM32 | Jan 2025 - Present
- Engineered a next-generation, innovation-driven IoT solution that redefines sustainable environmental sensing.
- Cut average current from 4.2 mA to 0.9 mA by sleeping between readings and batching radio transmissions.
- Published the schematics and firmware openly, and a local school built two stations from them.
Formula Student Electric Car | Electronics Lead, Team of 12 | C | Sep 2019 - May 2021
- Worked on firmware and testing for the robot fleet's motor controllers.
- The CAN-bus firmware for the dashboard was written and tested against the motor controller before each race.
- Rewrote motor-control firmware for a fleet of about 300 robots, cutting control-loop jitter eightfold and motor faults by more than half.
SKILLS
Tools: C, C++, STM32, oscilloscopes, FPGA
Methods: firmware, hardware-in-the-loop testing, CAN, low-power design

items.says: Place education below experience.
items.because: The degree was completed in 2021 and professional experience is stronger.

items.says: Verify that the portfolio URL is accessible and leads to relevant work.
items.because: A placeholder link should be removed.

items.says: Make the phone and email formatting consistent with the document.
items.because: Consistency improves scanability.

items.says: Add a relevant concentration, honor, or capstone if it strengthens the fit.
items.because: Generic coursework adds less than the professional experience.

items.says: Verify the June 2025 end date and use a current-date convention if still employed.
Identify the product or platform if Voltline is not recognizable.
items.because: Recruiters should quickly understand that the role was embedded robotics work.

items.says: Define what “update speed” measures.
items.because: It could mean download time, deployment time, bandwidth usage, or downtime.

items.says: Clarify which change produced the 60% result.
items.because: Combining compression and resumed downloads makes attribution unclear.

items.says: Add the scope or test conditions for the 60% result.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether it was measured across a fleet, device, or network condition.

items.says: Check that “interrupted downloads” wraps normally.
items.because: The final résumé should not use manually inserted line breaks.

items.says: State what the test rig improved.
items.because: The number of tests alone does not show coverage, defects found, or another effect.

items.says: Explain how the 400 tests ran and how long the suite took.
items.because: Their operational significance is unclear without that context.

items.says: Use consistent hardware-in-the-loop terminology.
items.because: The term also appears in Skills.

items.says: Say the logger enabled diagnosis rather than literally found root causes.
items.because: The logger may not have found the causes by itself.

items.says: Clarify whether the five failures were separate and how widely the logger was deployed.
Add the resulting fix or business impact if supported.
items.because: A reduction in recurrence or diagnosis time would show what the findings achieved.

items.says: An 8 kHz sampling rate cannot capture a 5 kHz signal without aliasing.
items.because: The rate must exceed twice the highest frequency component, with practical anti-alias filtering.

items.says: Clarify whether 5 kHz is the fundamental or highest relevant frequency.
items.because: The required sampling rate depends on the highest relevant component.

items.says: Describe the actual sampling, filtering, bandwidth, and detection decision.
items.because: The current engineering explanation should not be retained as written.

items.says: Declaring the counter volatile does not by itself fix a race condition.
items.because: Volatile does not make shared access atomic.

items.says: Identify the synchronization mechanism actually used.
items.because: Safety depends on interrupt timing and data-width constraints.

items.says: Reassess whether the bug was a race condition.
items.because: If access was naturally atomic, it may instead have been a visibility or optimization issue.

items.says: Add the main technical scope of the firmware rewrite.
items.because: The controller, architecture, real-time constraints, or subsystems are not clear.

items.says: Give the baseline or comparison period for field motor faults.
items.because: The reader needs to know how the reduction was measured.

items.says: Check whether the fault reduction was directly due to the rewrite.
items.because: Other simultaneous changes would make that causal claim too strong.

items.says: Specify what part of the end-of-line tests was automated.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether the work involved software, instruments, fixtures, or manufacturing integration.

items.says: Say whether the time reduction covers a complete station cycle or one step.
items.because: That changes how comparable the result is.

items.says: Use a consistent unit style for “a month.”
items.because: The review calls for one style throughout the résumé.

items.says: Give the time period and denominator for the return rates.
items.because: They could be monthly, quarterly, or cohort-level figures.

items.says: Make clear that the analysis led to the reflow-profile change.
items.because: The current line could leave open whether the two merely coincided.

items.says: Specify your role in updating the reflow profile.
items.because: Otherwise the line may overstate ownership.

items.says: Identify what kind of calibration drift complaints these were.
items.because: They could be customer complaints, internal reports, or service tickets.

items.says: Define the before-and-after period for the complaint reduction.
items.because: The number of quarters being compared is unclear.

items.says: Describe the calibration procedure’s scope if relevant.
items.because: It might cover instructions, settings, acceptance criteria, or software.

items.says: Clarify the grammar and units around “a quarter.”
items.because: The metric should plainly be a quarterly count.

items.says: Explain what enabled the throughput increase if useful.
items.because: It could have come from parallel testing, less setup time, or another fixture change.

items.says: Say whether throughput was theoretical, observed, or sustained in production.
Clarify its relationship to the end-of-line automation bullet if they were one project.
items.because: Separate accomplishments can appropriately remain separate.

items.says: Use a consistent format for the project technologies.
items.because: It is unclear whether “C, STM32” denotes languages, platforms, or tools.

items.says: Distinguish completed results from planned work in the ongoing project.
items.because: The power reduction, publication, and school deployment should be accurate as of the résumé date.

items.says: Replace the marketing language with a concrete technical detail.
items.because: The broad, unsupported phrasing says nothing about architecture, constraints, ownership, or impact.

items.says: Define the conditions used to measure average current.
items.because: Sampling interval, radio behavior, or methodology would make the result meaningful and reproducible.

items.says: Say whether the current is for the whole system or only the MCU.
items.because: That distinction matters for a low-power project.

items.says: Add a battery-life or operating-time result if it was calculated realistically.
items.because: It would show the effect of the current reduction under a realistic duty cycle.

items.says: Link directly to the repository if the portfolio URL does not.
items.because: The public schematics and firmware should be accessible.

items.says: Clarify your role in supporting the school builds, if any.
items.because: Documentation, troubleshooting, or assembly guidance would show your contribution.

items.says: Do not imply broad adoption from two builds.
items.because: Two stations demonstrate a concrete use, not large-scale impact.

items.says: Check whether the repository includes licensing information.
items.because: Open-source claims are stronger when the files are organized and licensed.

items.says: Reassess whether the Formula Student entry belongs on the résumé.
items.because: It overlaps the degree dates and contains material almost identical to Voltline, creating confusion.

items.says: Clarify the team size and your leadership scope.
items.because: It is unclear whether the 12 people were direct reports, electronics members, or the whole team.

items.says: “Robot fleet” conflicts with the Formula Student car project.
items.because: It makes the bullet look copied from Voltline.

items.says: Name the subsystem or responsibility you owned.
items.because: The bullet is too generic to show leadership or technical depth.

items.says: Clarify the testing context.
items.because: Race validation, bench testing, simulation, and integration imply different responsibilities.

items.says: Clarify what you wrote and what you tested.
items.because: The sentence does not establish whether you wrote dashboard firmware, tested the bus interface, or both.

items.says: Use “CAN bus” consistently with “CAN” elsewhere.
items.because: The terminology switches without an apparent style preference.

items.says: Specify your outcome or responsibility.
items.because: Reliability, validation, or diagnostics would be more informative if substantiated.

items.says: Explain your ownership of the pre-race process instead of relying on “before each race.”
items.because: That frequency may describe only a standard procedure.

items.says: The fleet firmware accomplishment duplicates the Voltline bullet.
items.because: Its wording, fleet size, and outcomes strongly suggest an accidental copy or inflated claim.

items.says: A fleet of robots conflicts with the single Formula Student car.
items.because: The project title describes a race car, not a robot fleet.

items.says: Separate languages, platforms, instruments, and hardware technologies.
items.because: They are mixed under “Tools.”

items.says: C and C++ are incorrectly listed as tools.
items.because: They are programming languages.

items.says: Categorize oscilloscopes as test equipment if retained.
items.because: They should not be presented as software tools.

items.says: Clarify the depth of the FPGA experience.
items.because: “FPGA” alone may invite questions about the HDL, environment, or device family used.

items.says: Firmware is incorrectly classified as a method.
items.because: It is a domain or type of development.

items.says: CAN is incorrectly classified as a method.
items.because: It is a protocol or technology.
